name: Charcoal Sketch
basis: why: powder sticks to paper bumps and slides off hollows; how: pressure against paper tooth, doubled outlines, smudge
note: Also offers conte, sanguine and graphite tints of the same model.

lumenary.blurb: A quick study in charcoal: dark tones catch on the tooth of the paper, thumbs smudge them, and the outlines are drawn twice.

facts.from: Drawing studios, and cave walls before that
facts.bestOn: Portraits and strong light and shade

why: Charcoal is a powder that sticks to the bumps of the paper and slides off the hollows, so whether a pixel turns black depends on the paper’s tooth as well as on the picture. A light touch catches only the peaks and shows grain, and a heavy one fills everything. Sketchy, doubled outlines and a smudged ground complete the hand-drawn feel.
how: Model the tooth of the paper as a mix of smooth and white noise.
Compute the stick’s pressure from the darkness of the lightly blurred picture, multiplied by the pressure slider and by diagonal streaks like a hand shading back and forth.
Ink the pixel where pressure beats the tooth, so light pressure only catches the peaks.
Read the edge map three times at places displaced by slow noise and keep the strongest reading, so outlines wander and double.
Add a heavily blurred copy as smudge, then tint everything as charcoal, conté, sanguine or graphite.
history: Charcoal is among the oldest drawing materials, used on cave walls for tens of thousands of years. Renaissance artists drew studies in red chalk, or sanguine, and Nicolas-Jacques Conté invented the conté crayon in 1795. Charcoal remains the standard material for quick figure studies, because it can be rubbed out and redrawn in a moment.
terms: The roughness of paper that grips the drawing material.
A red-brown chalk used for drawing, from the Latin for blood.
A hard drawing crayon made of pigment and clay, named after its inventor.
paragraphs: Charcoal is a powder that sticks to the bumps of the paper and slides off the hollows, so darkness alone does not decide whether a pixel turns black. The paper’s tooth does too. The program models the tooth as a mix of smooth and white noise (55% and 45%) and compares the stick’s pressure with it. The pressure itself is the darkness of the lightly blurred picture, multiplied by the pressure slider and by streaks: noise stretched along the 45 degree diagonal, which gives the direction of a hand shading back and forth. Where the pressure is high the stick reaches the hollows and the pixel is solid; where it is low only the peaks catch, and the grain shows.

The outlines are drawn more than once, the way a sketcher restates a contour. The edge map is read three times at places displaced by slow noise (2 to 12 px, from the sketchy-outlines slider) and the strongest reading wins, so lines wander and double. Smudging is a heavily blurred copy of the picture: dark regions dust the paper a little grey, as if a thumb had dragged the powder around. Four media are only different ink colours (charcoal, conté, sanguine and graphite), mixed over the paper by the final coverage.

equations.note: The paper tooth τ (smooth noise n, white noise r) decides which pressure values a_0 stick.
The redrawn outline: the edge strength E sampled at three noise-shifted positions.
a is the final coverage, w the smudge dusting taken from a blurred copy of the picture.

presets.text: Sanguine on cream paper looks like an old master study.
Heavy smudge and strong pressure make a moody drawing.
Graphite with light pressure feels like a quiet pencil sketch.
